not-the-end-of-the-world.summary: Hannah Ritchie, lead researcher at Our World in Data, argues that the data on air pollution, climate, deforestation, food, biodiversity, ocean plastics and overfishing shows real progress alongside real problems. She contends that humanity has never been sustainable in the full sense - meeting human needs while protecting the environment - but that ours could be the first generation to achieve it. The book replaces doom with 'urgent optimism' and focuses attention on the actions that matter most rather than well-meaning but low-impact ones.
takeaways: Sustainability has two halves: meet human needs and protect the environment
Ours could be the first generation to achieve both
Many rich countries have cut emissions while their economies grew
What you eat matters far more than how far it traveled
Nuclear and renewables are far safer than fossil fuels

cards.q: How does Hannah Ritchie define sustainability in Not the End of the World?
cards.a: Meeting everyone's needs today while leaving the environment fit for future generations
cards.explain: She argues no past generation has achieved both halves - earlier societies may have had small footprints but failed to meet basic human needs.
wrong: Keeping global population below a fixed planetary carrying capacity
Returning per-person consumption to pre-industrial levels everywhere
Reaching net-zero emissions in every country by 2050

cards.q: What is Ritchie's headline claim about our generation?
cards.a: We could be the first generation to achieve sustainability
cards.explain: Because living standards have risen and clean technologies are now cheap, she argues both halves of sustainability are within reach for the first time.
wrong: We are the last generation able to stop all warming
We are the first generation to cause environmental damage
We must accept lower living standards to be sustainable

cards.q: According to Ritchie, how much of a typical food's carbon footprint comes from transport?
cards.a: A small share - usually well under 10%
cards.explain: Land use and farm-stage emissions dominate, so 'eat local' matters far less than choosing lower-impact foods.
wrong: Exactly the same share as farming

cards.q: Per Ritchie, what is the single biggest dietary lever for cutting food emissions?
cards.a: Eating less beef and lamb
cards.explain: Ruminant meat has by far the highest emissions and land use per unit of protein; swapping it beats going local or organic.
wrong: Avoiding foods sold in plastic packaging

cards.q: What does Ritchie say about the safety of different energy sources?
cards.a: Nuclear and renewables cause far fewer deaths per unit of energy than fossil fuels
cards.explain: Most fossil fuel deaths come from air pollution, so coal, oil and gas are orders of magnitude deadlier per unit of electricity.
wrong: Nuclear is the deadliest source per unit of energy
Natural gas is the safest of all energy sources
All energy sources have roughly equal death rates

cards.q: Which environmental success does Ritchie use to show global problems can be solved?
cards.a: Repairing the ozone layer via the Montreal Protocol
cards.explain: Coordinated phase-out of ozone-depleting chemicals put the ozone layer on a path to recovery - proof that international action works.
wrong: Eliminating ocean plastics through the Basel Convention
Ending tropical deforestation through carbon markets
Stopping overfishing worldwide through the Kyoto Protocol

cards.q: What does Ritchie highlight about emissions in many rich countries such as the UK?
cards.a: They have fallen while their economies kept growing
cards.explain: This decoupling of CO2 from GDP undercuts the claim that cutting emissions requires economic decline.
wrong: They have risen in lockstep with economic growth
They only fell during recessions and then rebounded
They have stayed flat while their economies shrank

cards.q: Per Ritchie, where does most plastic entering the ocean come from?
cards.a: Mismanaged waste in middle-income countries plus fishing gear
cards.explain: Rich countries' waste is mostly landfilled or incinerated; much floating ocean plastic by mass is lost fishing nets and gear.
wrong: Plastic straws discarded in Europe and North America
Microplastics from synthetic clothing washed in rich countries
Plastic waste shipped by sea from the United States

how-to-avoid-a-climate-disaster.summary: Bill Gates argues the world must go from about 51 billion tons of greenhouse gases a year to zero, not merely reduce them. He breaks emissions into five activities - making things, plugging in, growing things, getting around, and keeping warm and cool - and shows that electricity is only part of the problem. His central tool is the 'Green Premium', the extra cost of the zero-carbon option, which he says must be driven down through innovation, policy and markets.
takeaways: The goal is zero, not just less: about 51 billion tons a year to net zero
Making things (cement, steel, plastics) is the largest emissions category
The Green Premium measures the cost gap between clean and dirty options
Electrify as much as possible and decarbonize the grid
Innovation must lower Green Premiums for hard sectors

cards.q: According to Gates, roughly how many tons of greenhouse gases does the world emit each year?
cards.a: About 51 billion tons of CO2-equivalent
cards.explain: Gates anchors the book on two numbers: 51 billion (where we are) and zero (where we need to go).

cards.q: What does Gates mean by the 'Green Premium'?
cards.a: The extra cost of choosing a zero-carbon option over a fossil one
cards.explain: Some premiums are already small or negative (e.g., some electricity); others, like cement or jet fuel, are large and need innovation.
wrong: A subsidy paid to fossil fuel producers to close plants
A tax rebate for households that install solar panels
The price premium consumers pay for organic food

cards.q: In Gates' breakdown, which activity is the largest share of emissions?
cards.a: Making things (cement, steel, plastics) at about 31%
cards.explain: Gates stresses that industry is bigger than electricity (about 27%), so clean power alone is not enough.
wrong: Keeping warm and cool at about 31%

cards.q: According to Gates, about what share of emissions comes from electricity ('plugging in')?
cards.a: About 27%
cards.explain: Electricity is crucial because cleaning it up also enables electrifying cars, heating and some industry.

cards.q: Why does Gates insist the target is zero rather than large reductions?
cards.a: CO2 lingers for centuries, so any continued emissions keep warming the planet
cards.explain: Because CO2 accumulates, temperatures stop rising only when net additions stop.
wrong: Because zero emissions automatically reverses past warming
Because the Paris Agreement legally requires zero by 2030
Because partial cuts make no difference to temperature at all

cards.q: Which question does Gates suggest asking of any climate plan, reflecting industry's importance?
cards.a: What's your plan for cement?
cards.explain: It is one of his five questions, a reminder that hard-to-abate materials are often ignored in plans focused on cars and power.
wrong: What's your plan for plastic straws?
What's your plan for paper bags?
What's your plan for light bulbs?

cards.q: According to Gates, roughly how much CO2 is released per ton of cement produced?
cards.a: About one ton of CO2
cards.explain: Heating limestone releases CO2 chemically as well as from fuel, which is why cement needs new process innovation.
wrong: Essentially none if using clean electricity

cards.q: What is Gates' broad strategy for most sectors?
cards.a: Decarbonize electricity and electrify as much as possible
cards.explain: Where electrification is impractical, he looks to clean fuels, carbon capture and innovation to lower the Green Premium.
wrong: Ban all fossil fuels immediately worldwide
Rely mainly on planting trees to offset emissions
Reduce global population to cut demand

speed-scale.summary: Venture capitalist John Doerr lays out an action plan to cut global emissions of about 59 gigatons CO2e to net zero by 2050, with roughly half the cuts by 2030. He applies OKRs (Objectives and Key Results) to six big objectives - electrify transportation, decarbonize the grid, fix food, protect nature, clean up industry and remove carbon - plus accelerators like policy, movements, innovation and investment. The book treats climate as an execution problem with measurable targets.
takeaways: Start from about 59 Gt CO2e per year and plan to net zero by 2050
Use OKRs: objectives plus measurable key results
Decarbonizing the grid is the biggest single objective
Carbon removal is needed for the residual emissions
Policy, movements, innovation and investment accelerate everything

cards.q: According to Speed & Scale, roughly how many gigatons of CO2e does the world emit per year?
cards.a: About 59 gigatons
cards.explain: Doerr uses this broader figure (including land use and all greenhouse gases) as the baseline for his net-zero plan.

cards.q: What management framework does Doerr apply to climate action?
cards.a: OKRs - Objectives and Key Results
cards.explain: Doerr popularized OKRs at Intel and Google; each climate objective gets measurable key results.

cards.q: What are Speed & Scale's timeline targets?
cards.a: Cut emissions about in half by 2030 and reach net zero by 2050
cards.explain: These milestones track IPCC pathways for limiting warming to about 1.5 degrees C.
wrong: Cut 10% by 2030 and reach net zero by 2100
Reach net zero by 2030 and go negative by 2035
Stabilize emissions by 2040 and cut half by 2070

cards.q: Which of the six big objectives in Speed & Scale offers the largest reduction?
cards.a: Decarbonize the grid
cards.explain: Clean electricity is the largest bucket because it powers both today's demand and the electrification of transport and heat.

cards.q: Roughly how many gigatons does Speed & Scale assign to carbon removal?
cards.a: About 10 gigatons per year
cards.explain: Removal (natural and engineered) handles residual emissions that cannot be eliminated by 2050.

cards.q: Which of these is one of Speed & Scale's six big objectives?
cards.a: Fix food
cards.explain: The six are electrify transportation, decarbonize the grid, fix food, protect nature, clean up industry and remove carbon.

cards.q: What are the 'accelerators' in Speed & Scale?
cards.a: Policy and politics, movements, innovation, and investment
cards.explain: They are cross-cutting levers that speed progress across all six sector objectives.

cards.q: What does the title 'Speed & Scale' stress about climate solutions?
cards.a: They must be deployed fast and at massive global scale
cards.explain: Doerr argues we have the core technologies; the challenge is deploying them quickly enough and widely enough.
wrong: They should be piloted slowly before any scaling
Speed matters more than total emissions reduced
Only small local projects can succeed

how-the-world-really-works.summary: Vaclav Smil explains the material and energy foundations of modern life - energy, food, materials, globalization, risk and environment - with an emphasis on quantities. He identifies four pillars of modern civilization (ammonia, steel, concrete/cement and plastics) that all depend heavily on fossil fuels. Smil argues that decarbonization is necessary but will be far slower and harder than many targets assume, and he positions himself as neither optimist nor pessimist but a scientist.
takeaways: Ammonia, steel, cement and plastics are the four material pillars
All four depend heavily on fossil fuels
Synthetic nitrogen fertilizer feeds roughly half of humanity
Fossil fuels still supply over 80% of primary energy
Energy transitions take decades, not years

cards.q: What does Smil call the four pillars of modern civilization?
cards.a: Ammonia, steel, concrete (cement) and plastics
cards.explain: Each is produced at enormous scale and depends heavily on fossil fuels as fuel or feedstock.

cards.q: Why does Smil consider ammonia arguably the most important material?
cards.a: Synthetic nitrogen fertilizer from ammonia feeds roughly half of humanity
cards.explain: Without Haber-Bosch nitrogen, Smil estimates the world could not feed about half its current population.
wrong: It is the main fuel for container ships today
It is the primary ingredient in concrete
It is the main feedstock for solar panels

cards.q: Which industrial process makes the ammonia Smil highlights?
cards.a: The Haber-Bosch process
cards.explain: It combines atmospheric nitrogen with hydrogen, today mostly derived from natural gas.

cards.q: What does Smil mean when he says we are, in effect, 'eating fossil fuels'?
cards.a: Modern food depends on fossil energy for fertilizer, machinery, and transport
cards.explain: Fossil inputs run through fertilizer, pesticides, farm machinery, irrigation, processing and distribution.
wrong: Most food now contains petroleum-based additives
Livestock are fed directly on crude oil byproducts
Crops absorb fossil carbon from polluted soil

cards.q: Per Smil, why is steelmaking hard to decarbonize?
cards.a: Blast furnaces rely on coke from coal to reduce iron ore
cards.explain: Carbon acts as both fuel and chemical reducing agent, so substitutes like green hydrogen must work at huge scale.
wrong: Steel can only be made with oil-fired furnaces
Steel plants are too small to electrify
Iron ore itself contains large amounts of methane

cards.q: According to Smil, roughly what share of global primary energy still comes from fossil fuels?
cards.a: Over 80%
cards.explain: Despite rapid growth of wind and solar, the fossil share has declined only slowly - a key reason he expects a long transition.

cards.q: What is Smil's view of net-zero-by-2050 targets?
cards.a: They are very unlikely given the scale and inertia of energy systems
cards.explain: He argues past transitions took decades and the material demands of modern life make rapid change very hard.
wrong: They will be easily met ahead of schedule
They are unnecessary because warming has stopped
They can be met through efficiency alone by 2030

cards.q: How does Smil describe his own stance on the future?
cards.a: Neither optimist nor pessimist - a scientist
cards.explain: He rejects both catastrophism and techno-optimism, emphasizing realistic understanding of how things work.

electrify.summary: Saul Griffith argues that the US can decarbonize mainly by electrifying almost everything - cars, home heating, water heating and cooking - and powering it with clean electricity. Because electric machines avoid the large thermal losses of burning fuels, an electrified economy needs roughly half the primary energy. He frames the challenge as replacing household machines at their end of life and as a financing problem, calling for cheap, long-term 'climate loans' and lower soft costs.
takeaways: Electrify everything and power it with clean electricity
Electrification cuts primary energy needs by roughly half
Every machine replacement is a climate decision
Cheap financing is as important as cheap technology
Soft costs make US rooftop solar far pricier than Australia's

cards.q: What is the core thesis of Saul Griffith's Electrify?
cards.a: Electrify nearly everything and power it with clean electricity
cards.explain: Cars, furnaces, water heaters and stoves become electric, and the grid shifts to wind, solar and other clean sources.
wrong: Capture carbon from every existing power plant
Cut energy use mainly through lifestyle sacrifice
Replace oil with hydrogen in all sectors

cards.q: Per Griffith, roughly how much less primary energy would a fully electrified US need?
cards.a: About half as much
cards.explain: Burning fuels wastes much energy as heat; electric motors and heat pumps are far more efficient.

cards.q: What does Griffith say is the key moment for household decarbonization?
cards.a: When each fossil-fueled machine is due for replacement
cards.explain: Since cars and furnaces last decades, every replacement must be electric to hit climate goals in time.
wrong: When a household moves to a new city
When energy prices hit record highs
When a new president takes office

cards.q: Why does Griffith call decarbonization largely a financing problem?
cards.a: Clean machines cost more upfront but less over time, so low-cost loans are key
cards.explain: He proposes cheap, long-term 'climate loans' like mortgages so households can afford upfront costs.
wrong: Because clean technologies are always more expensive to run
Because banks are legally barred from funding solar
Because fossil fuels have no upfront costs at all

cards.q: Why does Griffith say rooftop solar is far cheaper in Australia than the US?
cards.a: Lower soft costs like permitting, inspection and customer acquisition
cards.explain: The hardware is similar; US costs are inflated by red tape and paperwork.
wrong: Australian panels are made from cheaper materials
Australia has more sunlight on every roof
Australian installers are paid no wages

cards.q: Does Griffith argue Americans must give up big houses and cars?
cards.a: No - keep similar comforts but electrify them
cards.explain: He argues decarbonization needs no austerity; the same services can be electric.
wrong: Yes - homes must shrink by half
Yes - private cars must be banned
Yes - air conditioning must be phased out

cards.q: What nonprofit did Griffith co-found to promote household electrification?
cards.a: Rewiring America
cards.explain: It promotes electrifying homes and helped shape household incentives in US climate policy.

cards.q: Why are heat pumps central to Griffith's plan?
cards.a: They deliver several units of heat per unit of electricity
cards.explain: By moving heat rather than making it, heat pumps are 3-4 times more efficient than combustion heaters.
wrong: They run on natural gas more efficiently
They store electricity like a battery
They generate electricity from waste heat

the-new-map.summary: Daniel Yergin maps how energy shapes geopolitics, covering America's shale revolution, Russia's energy strategy, China's rise and its maritime concerns, the turbulent Middle East, and the climate-driven energy transition. He shows how shale turned the US into the world's largest oil and gas producer and changed the global balance of power. Yergin argues the transition will be complex and slower than many expect, with oil and gas remaining central for decades.
takeaways: Shale made the US the top oil and gas producer
Russia is pivoting energy exports toward China
China worries about chokepoints like the Strait of Malacca
OPEC+ reshaped oil market management after 2016
The energy transition will be gradual and contested

cards.q: According to The New Map, what transformed the US position in global energy?
cards.a: The shale revolution - fracking plus horizontal drilling
cards.explain: Shale made the US the world's largest oil and gas producer and an exporter, reshaping geopolitics.
wrong: Building dozens of new nuclear plants
Discovering vast new oil fields in Alaska

cards.q: Which two technologies combined to unlock US shale, per Yergin?
cards.a: Hydraulic fracturing and horizontal drilling
cards.explain: Together they made it economical to extract oil and gas from tight rock formations.
wrong: Carbon capture and enhanced oil recovery

cards.q: What is China's 'Malacca dilemma' described by Yergin?
cards.a: Its oil imports depend on a narrow strait that could be blockaded
cards.explain: Much of China's imported oil passes through the Strait of Malacca, a strategic vulnerability.
wrong: Its coal mines are concentrated in one province
Its solar panels depend on Malaysian silicon
Its rivers are too shallow for oil tankers

cards.q: What is 'Power of Siberia' in The New Map?
cards.a: A gas pipeline carrying Russian gas to China
cards.explain: It symbolizes Russia's pivot east as relations with Europe and the West deteriorated.
wrong: A hydropower dam on the Yenisei River

cards.q: What is OPEC+, as discussed by Yergin?
cards.a: An alliance of OPEC with non-OPEC producers led by Russia
cards.explain: Formed around 2016 to coordinate output against US shale and low prices.
wrong: OPEC's plan to invest in renewables
A US-led group of oil-importing countries
A futures market for Middle East crude

cards.q: What remarkable event in April 2020 does Yergin describe?
cards.a: US WTI oil futures briefly traded below zero
cards.explain: COVID-19 crushed demand and storage filled up, so sellers paid buyers to take oil.
wrong: Oil hit an all-time high above $200
OPEC dissolved after a price war
The US banned all crude exports

cards.q: Which colonial-era agreement does Yergin cite as shaping Middle East borders?
cards.a: The Sykes-Picot Agreement of 1916
cards.explain: This British-French deal divided Ottoman territories, leaving borders still contested today.

cards.q: What is Yergin's view on the pace of the energy transition?
cards.a: It will be gradual and complex, with oil and gas central for decades
cards.explain: He stresses that past transitions took a long time and that today's system is vast.
wrong: Fossil fuels will vanish within ten years
Oil demand already peaked permanently in 2010

the-price-is-wrong.summary: Economic geographer Brett Christophers argues that the falling cost of solar and wind is not enough to drive the energy transition, because investment depends on expected profitability, not price. In liberalized electricity markets, renewable revenues are volatile and low-margin, so private capital hesitates without subsidies or long-term contracts. He concludes that markets alone will not deliver decarbonization fast enough, and argues for a much larger role for the state, including public ownership.
takeaways: Profit, not cost, drives renewable investment
LCOE ignores revenue and market risk
Price cannibalization erodes renewable revenues
Long-term contracts and subsidies make projects bankable
Christophers calls for a bigger state role, including public ownership

cards.q: What is the central thesis of The Price Is Wrong?
cards.a: Profitability, not cheapness, determines whether renewables get built
cards.explain: Low costs mean little if expected revenues are uncertain or margins too thin for investors.
wrong: Renewables are still too expensive to compete
Fossil fuel subsidies are the only barrier
Consumers refuse to pay for clean power

cards.q: Why does Christophers critique LCOE as a guide to investment?
cards.a: It measures cost per MWh but says nothing about revenue or profit
cards.explain: A project with low LCOE can still be unprofitable if market prices are low or volatile.
wrong: It always overstates the cost of solar
It ignores fuel costs for gas plants
It only applies to nuclear power plants

cards.q: What is 'price cannibalization' for solar?
cards.a: When much solar generates at once, wholesale prices fall at those times
cards.explain: As solar grows, it depresses the prices solar itself earns at midday.
wrong: When solar firms undercut each other on panel prices
When utilities charge solar owners extra fees
When panel prices rise due to tariffs

cards.q: Per Christophers, why does the cost of capital matter so much for renewables?
cards.a: They are capital-intensive with no fuel cost, so financing dominates
cards.explain: Nearly all lifetime cost is upfront, so interest rates and risk premiums drive economics.
wrong: They require expensive fuel purchased in advance
They are financed only through equity, never debt
They have very short lifetimes of a few years

cards.q: How do PPAs and contracts for difference help renewables, in Christophers' analysis?
cards.a: They give stable, predictable revenue that makes projects bankable
cards.explain: Locking in a price reduces merchant risk, letting projects borrow on better terms.
wrong: They guarantee the lowest possible panel prices
They eliminate the need for grid connection
They let projects sell power above market price forever

cards.q: What kind of electricity markets does Christophers see as problematic for renewable investment?
cards.a: Liberalized wholesale markets with volatile prices
cards.explain: These were designed around fuel-burning plants and expose renewables to revenue risk.

cards.q: What policy direction does Christophers ultimately favor?
cards.a: A much larger state role, including public ownership
cards.explain: He argues private markets will not decarbonize fast enough without the state.
wrong: Removing all subsidies and letting markets decide
Taxing solar to fund fossil plants

cards.q: Why does Christophers argue subsidies and state support still matter even though solar is cheap?
cards.a: Without them, expected profits are often too low or uncertain to attract investment
cards.explain: His point is that low generation cost does not guarantee returns, so policy that de-risks revenue drives buildout.
wrong: Solar panels still cost more than coal plants to build
Subsidies are needed to pay for fuel costs
Banks are legally barred from financing renewables

short-circuiting-policy.summary: Political scientist Leah Stokes explains why US states have advanced, stalled or even rolled back clean energy laws such as renewable portfolio standards and net metering. She shows how electric utilities and fossil fuel interests, often aided by groups like ALEC, have fought to weaken these policies after enactment. Her key concept, the 'fog of enactment', explains why opponents often mobilize only after a law passes, leading to retrenchment, as in Ohio, Kansas and Arizona, while Texas shows how policies can succeed.
takeaways: Clean energy laws can be weakened after passage (retrenchment)
The 'fog of enactment' delays opposition until a law's effects are clear
Utilities have been central in fighting clean energy policy
ALEC spread model bills to repeal state RPS laws
Policy design and organized interests shape outcomes

cards.q: What is a Renewable Portfolio Standard (RPS), central to Stokes' book?
cards.a: A law requiring utilities to source a set share of power from renewables
cards.explain: RPS laws were the main US state clean energy policy and a target of utility opposition.
wrong: A tax credit for buying electric vehicles
A federal ban on new coal plants
A rule capping household electricity prices

cards.q: What does Stokes mean by the 'fog of enactment'?
cards.a: When laws pass, their impacts are unclear, so opponents mobilize later
cards.explain: Once costs and winners become clear, opponents organize to weaken the policy.
wrong: Lawmakers deliberately hide bills from the public
Pollution makes it hard to measure emissions
Voters forget a law once it is enacted

cards.q: What is 'retrenchment' in Short Circuiting Policy?
cards.a: Weakening or repealing a clean energy policy after enactment
cards.explain: Stokes documents retrenchment in states like Ohio, Kansas and Arizona.
wrong: Expanding a policy to new sectors
Transferring policy authority to the federal government

cards.q: Which state does Stokes present as an RPS success story, signed by George W. Bush?
cards.a: Texas
cards.explain: Texas's RPS (1999) helped spur a wind boom, and targets were met well ahead of schedule.

cards.q: What did Ohio do to its renewable standard in 2014, as described by Stokes?
cards.a: Froze it
cards.explain: Ohio's legislature paused its RPS amid pressure from utilities and fossil interests.

cards.q: What role does Stokes attribute to ALEC?
cards.a: It circulated model bills to repeal or weaken state RPS laws
cards.explain: ALEC connected corporate interests with legislators to spread anti-RPS legislation.
wrong: It funded new wind farms in the Midwest

cards.q: What is net metering, a policy fought over in Stokes' cases?
cards.a: Crediting rooftop solar owners for power they send to the grid
cards.explain: Utilities often push to weaken net metering because it reduces their sales.
wrong: Charging customers based on peak demand only
Metering emissions at power plant smokestacks
Capping how much power a home can use

cards.q: Why do utilities often oppose clean energy policies, per Stokes?
cards.a: They threaten utilities' business models and revenues
cards.explain: Rooftop solar and competition can reduce utility sales and investment returns.
wrong: Renewables are illegal for utilities to own
Utilities are legally banned from lobbying
Clean energy policies always raise utility profits

the-grid.summary: Anthropologist Gretchen Bakke tells the history of the American power grid, from Edison and the 'war of the currents' through Samuel Insull's regulated monopoly model to deregulation. She argues the grid was built for large, centralized, controllable power plants and is poorly suited to variable renewables and distributed generation. The book frames integrating renewables as a problem of balancing, storage and infrastructure as much as generation.
takeaways: The grid must balance supply and demand instantly
Insull's utility model favored big central plants and monopolies
Variable renewables strain a system built for dispatchable power
Aging infrastructure and weak maintenance cause blackouts
Storage and smarter grids are key to the future

cards.q: What fundamental constraint of the grid does Bakke stress?
cards.a: Supply and demand must be balanced in real time
cards.explain: With little storage, electricity must be generated as it is consumed.
wrong: Power can be stored cheaply for months
Only one power plant can run per region

cards.q: Who does Bakke credit with creating the regulated utility monopoly model?
cards.a: Samuel Insull
cards.explain: Insull built large central plants and accepted state regulation in exchange for monopoly territories.

cards.q: What was the 'war of the currents' covered in The Grid?
cards.a: Edison's DC versus Westinghouse and Tesla's AC
cards.explain: AC won because it could be stepped up for efficient long-distance transmission.
wrong: Public versus private ownership of utilities
Gas lighting versus electric lighting in homes

cards.q: What triggered the 2003 Northeast blackout, per Bakke?
cards.a: Lines hitting overgrown trees in Ohio plus an alarm software failure
cards.explain: Grid operators didn't see the problem in time, and failures cascaded to 50 million people.
wrong: A hurricane hitting New York City
A nuclear plant meltdown in Pennsylvania

cards.q: What did PURPA (1978) do, as described by Bakke?
cards.a: Required utilities to buy power from independent producers
cards.explain: It opened the grid to non-utility generation and set the stage for competition.
wrong: Banned the construction of nuclear plants
Created the federal tax credit for solar

cards.q: Why are variable renewables hard for the grid, per Bakke?
cards.a: The grid was designed for steady, controllable central plants
cards.explain: Wind and solar output fluctuates, requiring more flexibility, storage and transmission.
wrong: Renewables produce DC power that cannot be used
Renewables generate too much power at night
Renewables cannot connect to transmission lines

cards.q: Which crisis does Bakke cite as a deregulation failure?
cards.a: The California energy crisis of 2000-2001 with Enron manipulation
cards.explain: Market manipulation and flawed design led to blackouts and soaring prices.

cards.q: Which state does Bakke discuss as an example of high rooftop solar challenging its utility?
cards.a: Hawaii
cards.explain: High rooftop solar penetration on island grids forced the utility to confront new balancing challenges.

abundance.summary: Ezra Klein and Derek Thompson argue that many of America's problems - expensive housing, slow clean energy buildout, stalled infrastructure - stem from a scarcity created by policy and process. They criticize a liberalism that has prioritized procedures, lawsuits and veto points over results, and call for a politics focused on building more. In energy, they emphasize that permitting delays and transmission bottlenecks slow decarbonization even when money is available.
takeaways: Many shortages are policy choices, not inevitable
Process and veto points slow building
'Everything-bagel' programs pile on too many goals
Transmission and permitting are key clean energy bottlenecks
Government can build fast when focused on outcomes

cards.q: What is the core argument of Abundance?
cards.a: Many US shortages come from rules and process that block building
cards.explain: They argue scarcity in housing, energy and infrastructure is often self-inflicted.
wrong: Americans consume too much and must cut back
Markets alone will solve housing and energy

cards.q: What do Klein and Thompson mean by 'everything-bagel liberalism'?
cards.a: Loading programs with so many goals that they fail to deliver
cards.explain: Adding requirements to each program slows or stops the main objective.
wrong: Funding programs equally across all states
Offering free food in public programs

cards.q: Which law do the authors cite as enabling lengthy environmental reviews and litigation?
cards.a: The National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA)
cards.explain: NEPA reviews and lawsuits can delay projects, including clean energy and transmission.
wrong: The Clean Air Act Amendments of 1990

cards.q: Which project do the authors use as a cautionary tale of costly delays?
cards.a: California high-speed rail
cards.explain: Its costs ballooned and timelines slipped due to process and politics.

cards.q: What successful example of government speed do the authors highlight?
cards.a: Operation Warp Speed for COVID-19 vaccines
cards.explain: It showed government can deliver fast when focused on a clear goal.
wrong: The Affordable Care Act website launch

cards.q: Why is transmission a key clean energy bottleneck, per Abundance?
cards.a: New lines face years of permitting and local opposition
cards.explain: Without new lines, clean power can't reach demand, slowing decarbonization.
wrong: Transmission technology does not yet exist
Renewables do not need transmission lines
Transmission lines are banned in most states

cards.q: What do Klein and Thompson call their political vision?
cards.a: An abundance agenda: build more of what people need
cards.explain: They argue progress should be measured by how much housing, clean energy and infrastructure actually get built.
wrong: A degrowth agenda: consume and produce less
A deregulation agenda: abolish environmental law
A scarcity agenda: ration energy and housing

cards.q: Why do the authors say blue states struggle with housing costs?
cards.a: Zoning and regulations limit how much housing can be built
cards.explain: Restrictive rules constrain supply, raising prices and pushing people out.
wrong: Blue states have too much empty land
Federal law caps housing prices in blue states
Builders refuse to work in blue states

sustainable-energy-without-the-hot-air.summary: Physicist David MacKay teaches readers to evaluate energy claims with simple arithmetic, using kilowatt-hours per day per person as a common unit. He compares a 'consumption stack' with a 'production stack' of sustainable sources for the UK, showing that renewables have low power density and would require country-sized areas. MacKay concludes that any plan must add up, combining efficiency, electrification and large-scale supply from renewables, nuclear or imports.
takeaways: Use kWh per day per person for all energy
UK consumption is about 125 kWh/d per person
Renewables need large areas due to low power density
Small actions like unplugging chargers barely matter
Plans must add up: 'pro-arithmetic'

cards.q: What unit does MacKay use throughout the book?
cards.a: Kilowatt-hours per day per person (kWh/d)
cards.explain: It makes personal, national and technology comparisons intuitive.
wrong: Barrels of oil per year per country

cards.q: According to MacKay, roughly how much energy does the average UK person use?
cards.a: About 125 kWh per day
cards.explain: This includes transport, heating, electricity and embodied energy.

cards.q: What is MacKay's point about switching off phone chargers?
cards.a: It saves trivially little - like bailing the Titanic with a teaspoon
cards.explain: Chargers use about 0.01 kWh/d; he wants focus on big items like cars, heating and flying.
wrong: It is the most effective single energy action
It saves as much as giving up flying
It cuts household electricity use in half

cards.q: According to MacKay, about how much power per square meter do onshore wind farms deliver?
cards.a: About 2 watts per square meter
cards.explain: Low power density means wind would need huge land areas to supply much of UK demand.

cards.q: What is MacKay's famous line on his stance?
cards.a: I'm not pro-nuclear, I'm pro-arithmetic
cards.explain: He insists plans must add up, whatever mix of sources is chosen.

cards.q: How does MacKay compare UK energy demand with sustainable supply?
cards.a: Two stacks: consumption versus sustainable production
cards.explain: Stacking both in kWh/d shows the size of the gap that plans must close.
wrong: A pie chart of fuel costs by year
A ranking of countries by GDP
A list of renewable company profits

cards.q: Per MacKay, about how much energy does driving 50 km a day in an average car use?
cards.a: About 40 kWh per day
cards.explain: Car travel is one of the largest personal energy items.

cards.q: What is MacKay's main conclusion about renewables in the UK?
cards.a: They need country-sized areas, so plans must combine sources
cards.explain: Low power density means renewables alone would cover vast areas; efficiency and other sources are also needed.
wrong: They can easily supply all demand from rooftops
They are too expensive to ever be used
They produce more energy than the UK needs

drawdown.summary: Edited by Paul Hawken, Drawdown ranks 100 existing climate solutions by their potential to reduce or sequester greenhouse gases from 2020 to 2050. 'Drawdown' is the point when atmospheric greenhouse gas concentrations peak and begin to decline. The 2017 ranking surprised many: refrigerant management came first, and food, land and social solutions like reduced food waste, plant-rich diets, and educating girls ranked near the top alongside energy.
takeaways: Drawdown is when greenhouse gas concentrations peak and start declining
100 solutions are ranked by gigatons reduced, 2020-2050
Refrigerant management ranked first in 2017
Food, land and social solutions rank alongside energy
Educating girls and family planning together rank very high

cards.q: What does 'drawdown' mean in Hawken's book?
cards.a: When atmospheric greenhouse gases peak and begin to decline
cards.explain: It is the target point beyond simply reducing emissions.
wrong: When fossil fuel production hits zero
When global temperatures return to pre-industrial
When all countries sign a climate treaty

cards.q: Which solution ranked number one in Drawdown (2017)?
cards.a: Refrigerant management
cards.explain: HFC refrigerants are potent greenhouse gases; controlling leaks and disposal avoids huge emissions.

cards.q: Which agreement on HFCs relates to Drawdown's top solution?
cards.a: The Kigali Amendment to the Montreal Protocol
cards.explain: Adopted in 2016, it phases down HFC refrigerants.

cards.q: Which two food-related solutions ranked in Drawdown's 2017 top five?
cards.a: Reduced food waste and plant-rich diets
cards.explain: Food solutions ranked surprisingly high, ahead of many energy technologies.

cards.q: What social solutions together ranked very high in Drawdown?
cards.a: Educating girls and family planning
cards.explain: Combined, they affect population growth and resilience, ranking above any single solution.

cards.q: Which energy solution ranked highest in Drawdown (2017)?
cards.a: Onshore wind turbines
cards.explain: Onshore wind ranked second overall, the top electricity solution.

cards.q: How many solutions did Drawdown rank, and over what period?
cards.a: 100 solutions from 2020 to 2050
cards.explain: Each was modeled for gigatons avoided or sequestered over thirty years.

cards.q: What surprised many readers about Drawdown's rankings?
cards.a: Many top solutions were food, land and social, not energy
cards.explain: It broadened climate thinking beyond power plants and cars.
wrong: Every top solution was a new invention

doughnut-economics.summary: Kate Raworth proposes replacing GDP growth as the economy's goal with the 'Doughnut': meeting everyone's needs (social foundation) without overshooting planetary limits (ecological ceiling). The space between is the 'safe and just space for humanity'. She outlines seven ways to think like a 21st-century economist, including designing economies that are regenerative and distributive, and being agnostic about growth.
takeaways: Goal: a safe and just space between social foundation and ecological ceiling
Ecological ceiling is based on nine planetary boundaries
Replace GDP growth with meeting needs within limits
Design economies to be regenerative and distributive
Be agnostic about growth

cards.q: What is the Doughnut in Raworth's framework?
cards.a: A safe and just space between social needs and planetary limits
cards.explain: The inner ring is a social foundation; the outer ring is an ecological ceiling.
wrong: A model of circular recycling loops
A chart of GDP growth over time
A ring of trade routes around the globe

cards.q: What does the outer ring of the Doughnut represent?
cards.a: The ecological ceiling based on planetary boundaries
cards.explain: Overshooting it means exceeding limits like climate change or biodiversity loss.
wrong: The maximum GDP a country can reach
The social foundation of human needs

cards.q: How many planetary boundaries form the ecological ceiling?
cards.a: Nine
cards.explain: Developed by Rockstrom and colleagues, they include climate change, biodiversity loss and nitrogen cycles.

cards.q: What does the inner ring of the Doughnut represent?
cards.a: The social foundation of essential human needs
cards.explain: Falling short means deprivation in food, water, health, education and more.

cards.q: What is Raworth's first 'way to think' like a 21st-century economist?
cards.a: Change the goal from GDP growth to the Doughnut
cards.explain: She argues GDP growth is a poor goal; the aim should be thriving within limits.

cards.q: What is Raworth's stance on economic growth?
cards.a: Be agnostic about growth
cards.explain: Economies should thrive whether or not they grow, not be addicted to growth.
wrong: Growth is irrelevant to all policy

cards.q: Raworth critiques which model of human behavior?
cards.a: Rational economic man
cards.explain: She proposes seeing humans as social, reciprocal and adaptable.

cards.q: Which city notably adopted the Doughnut model in 2020?
cards.a: Amsterdam
cards.explain: Amsterdam used it to guide its post-pandemic recovery and circular economy plans.

cradle-to-cradle.summary: Architect William McDonough and chemist Michael Braungart argue that design should mimic nature, where 'waste equals food'. Rather than making products 'less bad' through eco-efficiency, they call for eco-effectiveness: products designed so materials circulate as biological nutrients returning safely to soil, or technical nutrients cycling in closed industrial loops. The book helped launch circular economy thinking and Cradle to Cradle certification.
takeaways: Waste equals food
Design for biological and technical nutrient cycles
Eco-effectiveness beats eco-efficiency
Downcycling is not true recycling
Use renewable energy and celebrate diversity

cards.q: What is the core principle of Cradle to Cradle?
cards.a: Waste equals food
cards.explain: Design products so materials become nutrients for new cycles instead of waste.

cards.q: What are the two material cycles in Cradle to Cradle?
cards.a: Biological nutrients and technical nutrients
cards.explain: Biological materials return safely to nature; technical ones cycle in closed industrial loops.

cards.q: How do McDonough and Braungart contrast eco-efficiency and eco-effectiveness?
cards.a: Eco-efficiency is less bad; eco-effectiveness aims to be good
cards.explain: Being 'less bad' is not being good - design should create positive impact.
wrong: Eco-efficiency is better because it is cheaper
Eco-effectiveness means using less energy only

cards.q: What do the authors call recycling that lowers material quality?
cards.a: Downcycling
cards.explain: Downcycling degrades materials over time, eventually ending in waste.

cards.q: What unusual material was Cradle to Cradle printed on?
cards.a: A synthetic, waterproof polymer 'paper'
cards.explain: It demonstrated a technical nutrient that could be recycled without degrading.

cards.q: What does 'cradle to grave' describe, according to the authors?
cards.a: A linear product life ending in landfill or incineration
cards.explain: They propose cradle to cradle as a cyclical alternative.

cards.q: Which energy principle do McDonough and Braungart advocate?
cards.a: Use current solar income
cards.explain: Rely on renewable energy flows like sunlight rather than stored fossil fuels.

cards.q: Which Ford facility do the authors highlight for a large green roof?
cards.a: The River Rouge plant
cards.explain: McDonough redesigned it with a living roof to manage stormwater.

saving-us.summary: Climate scientist Katharine Hayhoe argues that the most important thing people can do about climate change is talk about it. She explains how to connect with others through shared values rather than facts alone, noting that most people are not dismissive of climate science. Hayhoe emphasizes that many objections are smokescreens for fear of solutions, and that hope and practical action matter.
takeaways: Talking about climate is the most important action
Start with shared values, not facts
Only a small share of people are dismissive
Objections often hide fear of solutions
Hope comes from action

cards.q: What does Hayhoe call the most important thing to do about climate change?
cards.a: Talk about it
cards.explain: Conversations build awareness and social norms that drive action.

cards.q: What framework from Yale does Hayhoe use to describe public views?
cards.a: Global Warming's Six Americas
cards.explain: It segments people from Alarmed to Dismissive.

cards.q: About what share of Americans does Hayhoe say are dismissive?
cards.a: A small minority, roughly 10% or less
cards.explain: Most people are not dismissive, so they can be reached.

cards.q: How does Hayhoe recommend starting climate conversations?
cards.a: With shared values and connections
cards.explain: Connect on what people already care about, like family or faith.

cards.q: What does Hayhoe say many science objections really are?
cards.a: Smokescreens for fear of solutions
cards.explain: People often reject science because they dislike proposed policies.

cards.q: What is Hayhoe's professional background?
cards.a: Atmospheric scientist and evangelical Christian
cards.explain: Her faith helps her connect with religious communities.

cards.q: What does Hayhoe call climate change because it amplifies other problems?
cards.a: A threat multiplier
cards.explain: It worsens existing issues like poverty, health and conflict.

cards.q: Where does Hayhoe say hope comes from?
cards.a: From taking action, not from waiting
cards.explain: Action builds efficacy, and efficacy builds hope.

the-ministry-for-the-future.summary: Kim Stanley Robinson's novel follows a UN-linked agency created in 2025 to advocate for future generations, after a catastrophic heat wave in India kills millions. It explores policy innovations such as carbon coin, central bank action, geoengineering, glacier interventions, and also eco-terrorism. The book depicts a messy but ultimately hopeful path through climate change via institutions, finance and activism.
takeaways: A deadly heat wave triggers global urgency
Carbon coin rewards sequestration
Central banks help finance decarbonization
Geoengineering and glacier slowing appear
Hope comes from many messy actions

cards.q: What event opens The Ministry for the Future?
cards.a: A deadly heat wave in India killing millions
cards.explain: Extreme wet-bulb heat shows the stakes of climate change.

cards.q: What is the Ministry for the Future?
cards.a: An agency created to advocate for future generations
cards.explain: It is linked to the Paris Agreement and based in Zurich.

cards.q: Who leads the Ministry in the novel?
cards.a: Mary Murphy
cards.explain: She navigates politics, finance and activism.

cards.q: What is 'carbon coin' in the novel?
cards.a: A currency rewarding carbon sequestration
cards.explain: Central banks back it, paying for verified carbon drawdown.
wrong: A coin given to climate refugees

cards.q: What geoengineering does India attempt?
cards.a: Spraying aerosols into the atmosphere
cards.explain: It mimics volcanic eruptions to reflect sunlight.

cards.q: What intervention slows glaciers in the novel?
cards.a: Pumping water from beneath glaciers
cards.explain: Removing meltwater reduces sliding and sea-level rise.

cards.q: What role do central banks play in the novel?
cards.a: They back carbon coin and fund decarbonization
cards.explain: Monetary policy becomes a climate tool.
wrong: They print money for oil companies

cards.q: What darker form of activism appears in the novel?
cards.a: Eco-terrorism by a group called Children of Kali
cards.explain: They target polluters, adding pressure for change.
